background.definition: Gallstones are hard masses located in the gallbladder that are made of cholesterol (approximately 80% in adults; 20% in children), pigment (primarily calcium bilirubinate; 14%-20% in adults; 50% in children), or calcium carbonate (few in adults; 24% in children).

list.listitem: Based on 12 studies, the global incidence of gallstones was 0.47 per 100 person-years (95% CI, 0.37-0.51), with no differences between males and females. Since 2006, the incidence of cholelithiasis has been increasing, likely secondary to increasing obesity.
Among 1432 patients available for follow-up from 1530 morbidly obese patients who underwent laparoscopic bariatric surgery, the overall incidence of post-operative cholelithiasis was 9.7%.

Higher rates of post-bariatric surgery de-novo gallstone disease of 20.7% (95% credible interval [CrI] 13.0-29.7%; I2 = 75.4%) and symptomatic gallstone disease of 8.2% (95% CrI 5.9-11.1%; I2 = 66.9%) were reported in a systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis. Post-bariatric surgical risk of gallstones appears to be increased for females and those of Caucasian race.
Among 200 obese adolescents participating in an RCT comparing semaglutide once weekly to matching placebo (2 to 1 ratio), five subjects (4%) in the treatment group developed acute cholelithiasis.
In one prospective study, 5.1% of 42,705 men developed symptomatic gallstones over 16 years.
Among U.S. active armed service members during a 2014–2018 surveillance period, 8,008 had incident gallbladder disease for a crude overall incidence rate of 1.2 per 1,000 person-years.

Disorders of gallbladder and biliary tract were diagnosed in 0.4% (standard error 0.1%) or approximately 528,000 individuals presenting for emergency department visits based on the 2017 National Hospital Medical Ambulatory Care Survey.

Based on data from the Centers for Disease Control on non-federal short-stay US hospitals, there were 47,000 discharges for gallstones for patients aged 64 to 74 years between 2009 to 2010. This number has decreased from 61,000 in the year 2000.
In developed countries, gallstone prevalence ranges from 8% to 13% in men and 16% to 34% in women. Most patients have no symptoms.

Global pooled prevalence of gallstones based on a recent systematic review and meta-analysis including 115 studies with over 32 million participants was 6.1% (95% CI 5.6-6.5) and appeared to be stable over the past 20 years. Prevalence was higher in females vs males (7.6% vs 5.4%), in upper-middle-income countries vs high-income countries (8.9% vs 4.0%), and with advancing age.

Using ultrasound surveillance data, worldwide prevalence of gallstones for women was lowest in China, Japan and Thailand (4%-5%) and highest among Canadian and American Indian women (62%-73%), with white American women at 17% and Black American women at 14%.
According to healthgrades, the average 2017 U.S. cost for laparoscopic gallbladder surgery was $24,000; cost was $32,000 for open surgery.

Based on a retrospective observational cohort study of 372 laparoscopic cholecystectomy cases performed over one year by 12 surgeons from 3 different subspecialties, the average composite supply cost per case was $569, median case duration ranged from 70 to 107 minutes and average patient length of stay ranged from 1.15 to 3.10 days.
Mean unadjusted cost of a laparoscopic cholecystectomy for 3519 children in Canada (2008-2015) was $4115 (standard deviation $7273).

Gallstone disease contributes to approximately 2.2 million ambulatory care visits (2014-2016), 1.2 million emergency department visits (2019), 625000 hospital discharges (2019), and 2000 deaths annually based on National U.S. datasets.
Gallstones are the primary risk factor for biliary cancer (see prognosis).

Individuals with cholelithiasis are also more likely to develop cardiovascular disease, with a pooled hazard ratio of 1.23 (95% CI 1.16-1.30) for fatal and non-fatal CVD events based on 14 cohort studies with over 1.2 million participants. A somewhat higher relative risk of cardiovascular disease of 1.46 (95% CI 1.32-1.63) was reported in a more recent meta-analysis including 21 studies with over 2 million participants.

Based on 12 observational studies, the odds ratio of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease in a person with gallstone disease is 1.55 (95% CI 1.31-1.82). A similar OR of 1.5 (95% CI 1.3-1.6) was reported in a recent meta-analysis of 10 observational studies. These authors also found a higher risk of gallstone disease in those with NAFLD (OR 1.7, 95% CI 1.6-1.8) which could be attributed to the higher rates of female sex and high BMI among those with NAFLD compared to those without this condition.
Cholesterol stones form when there is an excess of cholesterol or an abnormal ratio of cholesterol, bile acids, and lecithin in the bile that causes supersaturation.

There is likely both a genetic and environmental component; in a paired-twin study, genetic effects accounted for 25%, shared environmental effects for 13%, and unique environmental effects for 62% of the phenotypic variance among twins.

In a genome-wide association study, loci in genes presumed to have functions in cholesterol metabolism and transport, and sulfonylation of bile acids or hydroxysteroids are associated with risk of gallstone disease.

Lower total cholesterol and higher triglyceride (TG) levels were two independent causal risk factors in a prospective study using UK biobank data. Interestingly, these authors found a decreased risk once serum TG levels exceeded 2.57 mmol/L. LDL-C and HDL-C were inversely associated with cholelithiasis risk in a linear fashion.
There is a positive association between H. pylori gallbladder infection and risk of chronic cholecystitis and cholelithiasis (OR 3.05, 95% CI 1.81-5.14, I2 23.5%).

While oral estrogen replacement therapy, which is metabolized by the liver, increases the risk of gallstones, the risk is much lower with transdermal hormone replacement (NNT 140). See table for risk factors.
Biliary dyskinesia has been thought to contribute to symptoms of cholelithiasis. However, it is common in healthy controls and there is no clear evidence that symptoms are improved after surgery.

Excess biliary cholesterol secretion can occur because of obesity, a high-cholesterol diet, clofibrate therapy, or with genetic predisposition; the excess cholesterol precipitates out of solution (nucleation), the crystals can then become trapped in gallbladder mucus (sludge) and grow to form cholesterol gallstones.
Genetic mutations can result in a reduction of bile acids and lecithin, predisposing some patients to gallstone formation.
Pigmented stones occur when increasing amounts of unconjugated bilirubin precipitate to form stones; this occurs in cases of high heme turnover, such as sickle cell anemia.
Gallbladder hypomotility with failure to empty supersaturated or crystal-containing bile is also a predisposing and perhaps necessary factor in stone formation.
Estrogen and Helicobacter species may also play a role.

list.listitem: Consumption of fruit and vegetables can help reduce gallstone disease. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis found both vegetable consumption (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.74-0.94) and fruit consumption (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.83-0.92) significantly associated with decreased gallstone disease risk with an absolute risk reduction of 4% and 3% for every 200 g per day increment in vegetables and fruits consumption, respectively.

Alcohol consumption is associated with a decrease in the overall risk of gallstone disease with a pooled RR of 0.84 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.89). However, this data needs to be interpreted cautiously given the myriad adverse health outcomes associated with alcohol use.

Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) 600 mg daily for 16 weeks may be useful in the prevention of gallstone formation in patients undergoing bariatric surgery. In a meta-analysis, the odds ratio was 0.43 (95% CI 0.22-0.83) with 8.8% of those using UDCA forming gallstones vs. 27.7% of those not using UDCA (NNT 5).

Similarly, in an RCT in Egypt of 1432 patients who underwent either sleeve gastrectomy, laparoscopic one anastomosis gastric bypass, or greater curve plication, the incidence of gallstones at one year was 22% in placebo arm compared to 6.5% in group receiving 6 months of UDCA (NNT =6). Patients who underwent sleeve gastrectomy were at significantly higher risk of gallstones (64.7 % vs. 28.1% and 7.2% with the other two procedures, respectively).

However, in an RCT of 967 patients undergoing bariatric surgery in the Netherlands, there was a trend in reduction in symptomatic gallstone disease for those randomized to 900 mg UDCA for 6 months that did not reach significance (6.5% vs. 9.7%, RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.43-1.04, p=0.071). There was a significant interaction between UDCA and the presence of asymptomatic gallstones at baseline; a positive effect of UDCA was seen in patients without gallstones at baseline (0.47, 0.27-0.84), but no effect in patients with baseline asymptomatic gallstones. Treatment effects were strongest in the group undergoing laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass. Adverse events were rare, confined to few patients with diarrhea or skin rash, and the number of serious adverse events did not significantly differ between groups.

Prophylactic concomitant cholecystectomy with bariatric surgery may be associated with a higher number of major postoperative complications compared to bariatric surgery alone (OR 1.74, 95% CrI 0.97-3.55; I2 = 56.5%). This was confirmed in a nationwide retrospective cohort study in which higher 90-day complication rates were found for concomitant cholecystectomy (OR 1.3, 95% CI 1.2-1.5), independent of the reason for cholecystectomy.
Authors of the UK Biobank study posit that HMGCR inhibition could be a future treatment to reduce the risk of cholelithiasis.

list.listitem: Patients with symptomatic gallstones usually have right upper quadrant or epigastric pain that sometimes radiates to the right shoulder, flank, or back and often occurs at night. Some patients only experience dyspepsia or indigestion. Biliary pain is usually episodic (biliary colic), lasting from 30 minutes to 5 hours.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 studies found a pooled prevalence of dyspepsia in 65.7% (95% CI 51-79%) of patients with gallstones, although only 3 studies used validated diagnostic criteria for dyspepsia and there was large heterogeneity across studies.
The overall clinical impression of a generalist physician is very specific but lacks sensitivity (33%) when evaluating patients with dyspepsia.
Pain may be precipitated by a fatty meal or a large meal followed by a prolonged fast.
Patients with CBD stones can present with biliary colic, obstructive jaundice, cholangitis, or pancreatitis. A clinical rule can predict the risk of CBD stones.

Ultrasound is a sensitive primary test in identifying cholelithiasis and cholecystitis and is the most appropriate test for evaluating right upper quadrant pain. However, cancer of the gallbladder cannot be ruled out with sonography. Computed tomography scan without contrast is also appropriate in patients with right upper quadrant pain of unknown etiology.

Ultrasound can also be used to identify biliary obstruction but is somewhat less accurate than a CT scan (LR+ 7.9 vs. 10.7). EUS, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP), and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) are more accurate tests for CBD stones.
Point-of-care ultrasound has high sensitivity (0.94, 95% CI 0.91-0.96) and specificity (0.93, 95% CI 0.91-0.95) for gallstones based on a meta-analysis of 7 studies including 1464 participants.

For patients with suspected biliary disease but negative or equivocal ultrasound and no fever or elevated white blood count, the American College of Radiology (2022) recommends magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen without and with IV contrast with MRCP, CT abdomen with IV contrast or MRI abdomen without IV contrast with MRCP as appropriate studies. When fever and elevated white blood count are also present, the most appropriate tests are MRI abdomen without and with IV contrast with MRCP, CT abdomen with IV contrast, or nuclear medicine scan of the gallbladder.

In patients with intermediate risk of choledocholithiasis, the American Society for Gastrointestinal Endoscopy (ASCE, 2019) suggests either EUS or MRCP given high specificity; other factors to consider include patient preference, local expertise, and availability.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE, 2014) recommends MRCP if ultrasound has not detected CBD stones but the bile duct is dilated and/or liver function results are abnormal. Authors of a systematic review found endosonography (EUS) and MRCP comparable in diagnostic accuracy, although MRCP performance may be decreased in overweight and obese patients. Given its risks, however, ERCP should primarily be considered a therapeutic procedure and should not be used for routine diagnosis prior to cholecystectomy.

No benefit to the routine use of intraoperative cholangiography was found in a systematic review of 8 trials; however, the trials were underpowered. NICE recommends clearing the bile duct surgically at the time of laparoscopic cholecystectomy or with ERCP before or at the time of surgery.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 20 RCTs with 2489 patients with gallstone disease with biliary duct calculi who were undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy concluded that use of intraoperative ERCP resulted in the highest success rates and safety with respect to morbidity compared with pre- or post-operative ERCP or common duct exploration. There were no differences in mortality.

If CBD stones are clinically suspected, EUS and MRCP are both highly accurate tests. Both ASGE and the updated British guidelines suggest using one of these two tests in patients with intermediate likelihood of CBD stones (CBD dilation with normal liver function tests or abnormal liver function with a normal caliber biliary system) and proceeding to ERCP or surgical extraction for those at high suspicion of CBD stones. Percutaneous radiological techniques can be used if stones can’t be extracted with surgery or ERCP. CT can be considered prior to surgery if malignancy is suspected.
In patients with gallstone pancreatitis without cholangitis or biliary obstruction/ choledocholithiasis, ASGE recommends against urgent (<48 hours) ERCP.

Laboratory tests are not usually helpful, but an elevated direct bilirubin or GGT level suggests a CBD stone, while a normal GGT level makes it unlikely (negative predictive value = 98%). In a retrospective study of adult patients with acute cholecystitis or biliary colic, an elevated total bilirubin level at presentation was associated with CBD stones (3.74 mg/dl vs. 2.29 mg/dl in patients without CBD stones).

Among patients with pancreatitis, an abnormal AST level plus either an elevated bilirubin or alkaline phosphatase levels suggest cholelithiasis as the cause. Among patients presenting with gallstone pancreatitis, MRCP is the most accurate test for diagnosis of CBD stones.

A clinical decision rule has been developed and validated to predict the likelihood of CBD stones. Patients with no jaundice, normal transaminase levels, CBD diameter less than 8 mm, and no intrahepatic duct enlargement on conventional ultrasound are at low risk (1/168 or 0.6% with CBD stones); all others were higher risk (42/108 or 39% with CBD stones).

Not all patients with symptomatic uncomplicated gallstones benefit from cholecystectomy with respect to clinically-relevant pain reduction. In a Dutch study including 494 patients in 7 hospitals in the development cohort and 1067 patients in 24 hospitals in the validation cohort, a multivariable prediction model showed that increased age, no history of abdominal surgery, increased visual analog scale pain score at baseline, pain radiation to the back, pain reduction with simple analgesics, nausea, and no heartburn were independent predictors of clinically-relevant pain reduction after cholecystectomy (C statistic 0.80, 95% CI 0.74-0.84 and 0.74, 95% CI 0.70-0.78 in the external validation model). The tool has good discrimination and calibration and is available as an external online calculator.
Another rule predicts the likelihood of conversion from laparoscopic to open cholecystectomy. A limitation to this rule is that it was validated in residents undergoing training.

Opiates can be given to patients presenting with acute abdominal pain without increasing risk of management errors. Authors of a meta-analysis, however, found intramuscular or intravenous NSAIDs (primarily diclofenac) more effective than placebo or spasmolytics for biliary colic and as effective as opioids to treat pain in patients with biliary colic.

Authors of a Cochrane review evaluating NSAIDs for biliary colic found that NSAIDs were better than placebo for pain relief (moderate quality evidence). Of the 12 RCTs included in the analysis, only 1 RCT was deemed to be at low risk of bias, and none of the studies reported quality of life measures. The authors recommended caution when generalizing these results, adding there were very few older adults and complicated patients included in the trials.
An RCT did not find benefit on postoperative pain for either preoperative rofecoxib or bupivacaine infiltration or both.

Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) can be considered in patients with either asymptomatic or symptomatic gallstones; in one cohort study of 527 patients, UDCA was associated with reduced biliary pain at 10 years in both asymptomatic (6% vs 12%; NNT 17) and symptomatic (62% vs 92%; NNT 3) patients, regardless of stone dissolution. Risk for conversion to cholecystectomy (frequent attacks or cholecystitis) was also decreased in symptomatic patients (26% vs 88%; NNT 2). Dissolution of the gallstone was more likely to occur with small stones (<10 mm), radiolucency, and visualized gallbladder on oral cholecystogram (functional gallbladder).

Prophylactic antibiotics do not appear necessary for low-risk patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy. A Swedish population-based study confirmed that prophylactic antibiotics did not benefit patients undergoing acute cholecystectomy.

A clinical prediction rule was developed in 1561 patients and prospectively validated in 1067 with the goal of identifying patients most likely to benefit symptomatically from cholecystectomy. It has good discrimination and calibration and is available as an external online calculator.

Symptomatic cholelithiasis is usually managed with surgery, but findings of a systematic review reported only 1 RCT of surgery versus observation which found no difference between these two approaches in terms of gallstone-related events (eg, pain attacks, complications) at 5 or 14 years, along with comparable quality of life outcomes (also see Watchful Waiting below).

For patients with symptomatic gallstones who elect surgery, both laparoscopic cholecystectomy and small-incision cholecystectomy are associated with shorter hospital stays, quicker time to recovery, and similar complication rates compared with open cholecystectomy. Laparoscopic cholecystectomy and small-incision cholecystectomy are equivalent with respect to mortality, complications, and postoperative recovery for patients with symptomatic cholelithiasis; the latter requires significantly shorter operative time.

In an RCT of 187 patients with symptomatic cholecystolithiasis, those randomized to single incision vs. 3-port laparoscopic surgery had 13-minute shorter operative times, higher success rates (99% vs 93%, respectively) and superior aesthetic results. Three- and four-port laparoscopic cholecystectomies appear comparable with respect to procedural and morbidity outcomes.

In an RCT including 100 patients, reducing the pressure applied during laparoscopic cholecystectomy from 12 mmHg to 8 mmHg reduced postoperative recovery room fentanyl requirement and post-operative nausea and vomiting, although visibility was also reduced which required pressure to be increased more often in the 8-mmHg group (29% vs. 8%).

Needlescopic cholecystectomy is a refinement of the laparoscopic procedure in which instruments and ports smaller than 3 mm in diameter are used compared with the standard 5-mm and 10-mm sizes used in conventional laparoscopic cholecystectomy. In an RCT of 105 patients undergoing cholecystectomy, surgical outcomes and cosmetic appearance were similar for those randomized to needlescopic cholecystectomy vs. conventional laparoscopic cholecystectomy but there was less day-one incisional post-operative pain in the needlescopic group.

In one retrospective study of 346 patients, preoperative risk factors associated with need for conversion from laparoscopic to open cholecystectomy were advanced age, male gender, previous upper abdominal surgery, preoperative diagnosis of acute cholecystitis, and pericholecystic fluid. The authors recommended an open procedure for patients who have all of these risk factors.
A robotic assistant for cholecystectomy is safe, but seems to offer no clear advantages over a human assistant.

Abdominal wall lift with or without pneumoperitoneum for laparoscopic cholecystectomy in people with low anesthetic risk offers no advantages over pneumoperitoneum alone with respect to patient-oriented outcomes.

Subtotal cholecystectomy is used in cases of severe cholecystitis when structures of the Calot triangle cannot be safely identified. In one systematic review of studies, morbidity rates were relatively low (postoperative hemorrhage, 0.3%; bile duct injury, 0.08%; and retained stones, 3.1%), although the rate for bile leaks was 18%. Reoperation occurred in 1.8% of the cases and the 30-day mortality rate was 0.4%.
Cholecystolithotomy (removal of gallstones from the gallbladder)

In a prospective study of 216 Chinese patients, most (81%) with a single symptomatic gallstone, 200 were symptom free post-operatively and 20 (9.3%) developed recurrent gallstones during the follow-up period, most within 2 years, with no differences in recurrence with use of 6 or 12 months of UDCA.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 studies with 1663 participants found a higher risk of recurrent gallstones for patients undergoing cholecystolithotomy for those with a family history of cholelithiasis (OR 3.28), multiple calculi (OR 4.24), gallbladder wall thickening over 3 mm (OR 18.4), a preference for greasy food (OR 1.9), dysfunction of the gallbladder (OR 26.16), and not taking oral UDCA post-procedure (OR 2.90).

For patients with acute calculous cholecystitis, a meta-analysis demonstrated that early (within 7 days) open or laparoscopic surgery was associated with similar mortality and morbidity as delayed surgery (6-12 weeks after symptoms), but shorter hospital stays.

Authors of a Cochrane review found only a single high-bias trial demonstrating that early laparoscopic cholecystectomy (less than 24 hours after diagnosis of biliary colic) decreased morbidity during the waiting period for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy (mean waiting time 4.2 months) as well as hospital stay and operating time.

Another meta-analysis of 40 RCTs (39 of which were used in the meta-analysis) concluded that early cholecystectomy (within 7 days) may have fewer biliary complications and better abdominal pain reduction compared to conservative management plus delayed cholecystectomy (after 6 weeks).

Similarly, for mild biliary pancreatitis (8 cohort studies and two RCTs), index admission cholecystectomy is associated with lower risk of readmission for recurrent biliary events (eg, recurrent biliary pancreatitis) than interval cholecystectomy.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 19 studies with 2639 patients with mild gallstone pancreatitis found early laparoscopic cholecystectomy comparable to delayed laparoscopic cholecystectomy for intra- or postoperative complications, conversion rate, operative time and readmission rate; although there were fewer gallstone-related events and lower length of stay with the early approach.

Similarly, authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs with 629 patients with mild gallstone pancreatitis found the early approach reduced recurrent biliary events requiring hospitalization but no other differences in intra- or postoperative complications compared to delayed cholecystectomy. In a recent RCT including 198 patients with a first episode of mild acute biliary pancreatitis, surgery within 7 days compared to 4 weeks reduced the rate of readmissions for biliary events before cholecystectomy (7.2% vs 15.8%, respectively), but also found no differences in type of surgery, postoperative stay, or complications.

However, in a retrospective cohort study including 3696 patients with acute biliary pancreatitis of whom 32.5% underwent early (within 48 hours) and 2494 underwent delayed cholecystectomy, early surgery was associated with an increased risk of mortality (1.4% vs 0.1%) and morbidity (7.7% vs 3.7%) compared with delayed surgery. This difference was magnified for the 108 patients with moderate to severe acute biliary pancreatitis who underwent early surgery compared to those with mild biliary pancreatitis undergoing early surgery (mortality 15.6% vs 0%, respectively, and morbidity 30.3% vs 5.5%, respectively).

Using the Nationwide Inpatient Sample database including 6,662 patients with sickle cell disease who presented with cholelithiasis, those with a more advanced presentation (73%) had a higher risk of perioperative vaso-occlusive crisis, the most common complication. Compared to patients undergoing cholecystectomy for uncomplicated cholelithiasis, the risk was higher for those with acute cholecystitis (OR 2.4, 95% CI 1.6 to 3.4), chronic cholecystitis (OR 1.7, 95% CI 1.3 to 2.4), and choledocholithiasis or gallstone pancreatitis (OR 2.2, 95% CI 1.4 to 3.6). This implies benefit for those undergoing cholecystectomy earlier in their disease course.

The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE, 2014) recommends offering early (within one week) laparoscopic cholecystectomy to people with symptomatic gallstones or acute cholecystitis.

Based on 5 RCTs, day-case elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy ("day surgery") for symptomatic gallstones is a safe and effective option in selected cases. In one RCT of 88 patients with non-complicated symptomatic gallstone disease, day-case minilaparotomy cholecystectomy with ultrasonic dissection technique showed similar one-year results as laparoscopic cholecystectomy with respect to residual abdominal symptoms, cosmetic satisfaction, and quality of life for the 78 who were reached for follow-up.

In one before and after study, implementation of an acute care surgery model (attending surgeon without other duties and one or two residents) reduced time to operating room, hospital length of stay by about half a day, and complication rates (18.5% before and 7% after) for patients with uncomplicated acute cholecystitis. Authors do not report whether chart auditors were blinded to time period.

Fast track refers to a multimodal approach to patient care using a combination of evidence-based perioperative interventions to expedite recovery after surgery primarily to reduce length of hospital stay. Interventions may include preoperative counseling; bowel preparation; carbohydrate loading; prophylaxis with antibiotics and for post-operative nausea and vomiting in the presence of risk factors; use of standard anesthetic protocols; maintaining vital signs and avoiding fluid overload; good post-operative pain control; early mobilization and oral intake; and quality improvement. In a small RCT including 30 patients with cholelithiasis undergoing planned cholecystectomy, those randomized to fast track vs. standard care treatment protocol had a higher rate of treatment success (OR 3.1; 95% CI 0.2-6.0).

In one large case series of 2,714 patients without suspected common bile duct (CBD) stones undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy, fifty-five cases (2%) were converted to open surgery, five cases (0.18%) had major bile duct injuries requiring surgical repair, postoperative bile leakage occurred in seven cases (0.26%) and missed CBD stones were reported in six cases (0.22%). There was no perioperative mortality.

In a small RCT, spinal anesthesia vs. general anesthesia for laparoscopic cholecystectomy was associated with less early postoperative pain (no difference at 12 hours), lower cost and higher patient satisfaction. In another RCT of 180 patients, spinal vs. general anesthesia was associated with less postoperative pain and a lower incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (resulting in overnight stay) but no difference in patient satisfaction.

In a 4-arm RCT with 160 adult patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy for cholelithiasis, perioperative local anesthetic administration methods of local injection at trocar access points, intraperitoneal local anesthetic injection, or transversus abdominis plane block were more effective in preventing post-operative pain than no local anesthetic administration. Intraperitoneal injection was less effective than the other two two treatment arms.

In an RCT of 92 patients (of an original 106), use of intraperitoneal mesh vs. suture closure of the umbilical trocar site resulted in fewer Trocar site incisional hernias (4.4% vs 31.9%), fewer wound infections (8.5% vs 0%), and possibly less postoperative pain. Long-term complications are not known.

Between 10% and 18% of patients undergoing cholecystectomy for gallstones have CBD stones. A clinical rule can predict their likelihood. In 2019, the ASGE modified the individual predictors of choledocholithiasis proposed in the 2010 guideline by removing the weakest predictors to improve predictive performance. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 20 studies investigating these predictors found that a stone identified on ultrasound had the strongest performance with a mean sensitivity of 37%, specificity 94%, PPV 81%, and NPV 62%. CBD >6 mm demonstrated the highest sensitivity at 76%, but lower specificity of 48%. Moderate predictors, including acute cholangitis, abnormal liver function tests, total bilirubin >4mg/dL, and age >55 years had inconsistent and/or weak performance, and gallstone pancreatitis was non-predictive of choledocholithiasis.

Options for management in these cases include open or laparoscopic surgery, preoperative or postoperative endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP, a combination upper endoscopy and fluoroscopy with injection of dye into the biliary and pancreatic ducts; if needed, sphincterotomy can be performed to remove stones), balloon dilation, or lithotripsy (the latter two are discussed in other treatment).

Initial cholecystectomy with intraoperative cholangiogram compared to sequential common duct endoscopy followed by surgery for patients at intermediate risk of choledocholithiasis led to shorter hospital length of stay and similar outcomes in a randomized trial of 100 patients.

Extraction should be offered to patients with CBD stones. Patients with acute cholangitis not responding to antibiotics or who are in septic shock should have urgent decompression of the biliary tract with endoscopic extraction with or without biliary stent.

In an RCT of 70 patients with patients with concomitant cholelithiasis and choledocholithiasis who had evidence of clearance of choledocholithiasis, there was a higher complication rate with prophylactic stenting and no benefit was observed in preventing choledocholithiasis recurrence in patients waiting for cholecystectomy after biliary clearance.

Open procedures: In cases of CBD stones, open bile duct exploration may be needed when ERCP fails and laparoscopic exploration is not feasible. In these cases, primary closure is preferred over T-tube drainage and results in shorter operating time and hospital stay but no other differences in clinically-important outcomes. Investigators in a small RCT of 60 patients found choledochotomy closure vs. stent vs. T-tube resulted in a shorter postoperative stay and an earlier return to normal activity.

Primary duct closure with or without biliary stenting was also found to be superior to T-tube drainage in overall morbidity, incidence of bile leak and bile peritonitis, shorter surgical time, and reduced postoperative hospital stay based on a meta-analysis of 26 studies with 2552 patients with choledocholithiasis.

Authors of a Cochrane review found that open bile duct surgery was superior to ERCP in achieving clearance of CBD stones, while laparoscopic CBD stone clearance was comparable with ERCP; ERCP however necessitates additional procedures.

For patients with CBD stones, authors of a meta-analysis of 19 RCTs with 2466 patients found no differences between CBD surgery and ERCP on mortality, bile duct clearance failure, complications and length of hospital stay; quality of evidence was low.

ERCP: Authors of an RCT of 104 patients with choledocholithiasis undergoing emergency laparoscopic cholecystectomy found that the rate of retained stones was lower in the group receiving ERCP compared to laparoscopic bile duct exploration (15% vs 42%, respectively) and length of hospital stay was shorter by 1 day. However, authors of a meta-analysis of 11 RCTs found that the two procedures were both highly effective in detecting and removing CBD stones and were equivalent in complications.

Although authors of a meta-analysis of 12 RCTs with 1545 patients also found that an intraoperative procedure, in this case laparoscopic CBD exploration, plus laparoscopic cholecystectomy shortened hospital stay (mean difference − 2.46 days; 95% CI − 3.67 to − 1.24), preoperative ERCP plus laparoscopic cholecystectomy was associated with a higher CBD stone clearance rate (OR 1.63; 95% CI 1.16–2.28) and lower postoperative bile leakage rate (OR 4.08; 95% CI 2.08–7.98), although the rate of pancreatitis was higher in these patients (OR 0.23; 95% CI 0.11–0.50). Mortality and overall morbidity rates were similar.

Transcystic approach: Exploration of the CBD can also be achieved intraoperatively through a transcystic duct approach using the lumen of the cystic duct to avoid the need to open the CBD or a choledocal approach. Authors of one meta-analysis of 25 studies with 4224 patients found laparoscopic transcyctic exploration compared to laparoscopic choledochotomy achieved a lower duct clearance rate (OR 0.38, 95 % CI 0.24-0.59) but was associated with a shorter duration of surgery, lower bile leak (OR 0·46, 0·23 to 0·93), and shorter hospital stay (MD -0.78, 95% CI -1·14 to -0·42).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 30 studies with 4073 patients found similar duct clearance rates between the two procedures with lower overall complications, biliary complications, and blood loss for the transcystic compared to the transductal approach.

Sphincterotomy: Authors of a meta-analysis of 4 trials of patients with cholelithiasis and suspected CBD stones, found intraoperative endoscopic sphincterotomy as effective and safe as preoperative endoscopic sphincterotomy, with the former associated with significantly shorter hospital stay (3 days) and potentially fewer complications.

In an RCT including 77 patients with concomitant gallstones and CBD stones, quality-of-life scores were comparable for patients randomized to either laparoscopic CBD exploration with cholecystectomy or endoscopic sphincterotomy followed by laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

In another meta-analysis of 13 studies of patients with both gallstones and CBD stones undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy, stone clearance rate, however, was higher for those undergoing laparoscopic common bile duct exploration compared to preoperative endoscopic sphincterotomy (94.1% vs 90.1%, respectively) and associated with lower rates of perioperative complications (7.6% vs 12.0%), conversion to other procedure (4.1% vs 7.1%), and retained stones rate (1.2% vs 7.9%).

Cholangioscope: Single-operator peroral cholangioscope is an option for difficult biliary stones with one author reporting a pooled proportion of patients with complete stone clearance of 94.3% (95% CI 90.2-97.5), pooled number of sessions needed for stone clearance of 1.26 (95% CI 1.17-1.34) and pooled adverse event rate of 6.1% (95% CI 3.8-8.7) based on 24 studies with 2786 patients.

Biliary dyskinesia (BD) is not considered a clear indication for surgery in adults as it occurs in 20% of healthy controls and an even higher number of patients with various other disorders. One small RCT compared cholecystectomy to no surgery for 21 patients with BD. After 34 months all patients in the surgery group and only one paient in the control group experienced improvement in symptoms. However, the trial was unblinded and morbidity due to the procedure was not reported. A retrospective cohort study (uncontrolled) found a clinical response in 88% of patients after a mean of 65 months follow-up, but this study is at high risk of bias.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 RCTs with uncertain risk of bias concluded that use of traditional Chinese medicine may reduce the recurrence rate after gallbladder-preserving lithotripsy.
A Cochrane review found no conclusive evidence that the reviewed Chinese medicinal herbs were effective for asymptomatic or mild-to-moderate cholelithiasis.

The presence of asymptomatic gallstones is not a clear indication for cholecystectomy unless there is a concern for malignancy (eg, calcified gallbladder wall or family history of gallbladder cancer). Unfortunately, there are no RCTs comparing cholecystectomy with no cholecystectomy for silent gallstones. NICE recommends that people with asymptomatic gallstones, a normal gallbladder, and normal biliary tree be reassured that they do not need treatment unless they develop symptoms.
Asymptomatic gallstones can be managed expectantly; symptoms develop in only 1% to 2% per year and there are few complications (3%).

In one study, only 35 of 69 patients (51%) with symptomatic gallstones randomized to observation eventually had surgery after a median of 5.6 years. In two small Norwegian RCTs, 45% of those randomized to observation eventually underwent surgery by 14 year follow-up.

In a non-inferiority (SECURE) RCT conducted in the Netherlands of 1067 adults with abdominal pain and ultrasound-proven gallstones or sludge, the proportion of patients who were pain-free at 12 months' follow-up was slightly higher (non-inferiority not shown) using usual care in which selection for cholecystectomy was left to the surgeon’s discretion compared to a restrictive approach in which patients were only recommended for surgery if they meet five criteria: severe pain attacks, pain lasting 15-30 min or longer, pain located in epigastrium or right upper quadrant, pain radiating to the back, and a positive pain response to simple analgesics (60% vs 56% pain free). The usual approach, however, resulted in more cholecystectomies (75% vs 68%) with no differences in trial-related gallstone complications, surgical complications or non-trial-related serious adverse events.

In a 5-year telephone follow-up of patients in the SECURE trial, (response rate 491 of 537 patients [91.4%] in the usual care group and 479 of 530 patients [90.4%] in the restrictive strategy group), the restrictive strategy resulted in a significant but small reduction in operation rate of 8.3% compared with usual care (73.2% vs 81.5%, respectively). There were no differences in biliary or surgical complication rates or patient satisfaction between groups. When detailed information about pain status was obtained from about two thirds of the patients who responded to an email survey, there were no differences in the proportion of patients who were pain free by group (62.8% usual care vs. 61.2% restrictive care) or in the proportion of patients pain free following cholecystectomy by group assignment (187 of 294 patients [63.6%] in the usual care group and 160 of 254 patients [63.0%] in the restrictive care group).

In a UK RCT of 434 patients with symptomatic uncomplicated gallstone disease randomized to either laparoscopic cholecystectomy or observation/conservative management, 70.5% vs. 29.5% had received surgery at a median of 4.7 and 9 months, respectively, with no differences in bodily pain scores, quality of life, complications or need for further treatment at 24 months. Condition-specific quality of life at 24 months favored cholecystectomy with a mean difference 9.0 (95% CI 4.1-14.0) with a similar pattern for the persistent symptoms score.

Authors of a systematic review only found 1 RCT evaluating surgery versus observation which found no difference between the two in terms of gallstone-related events (eg, pain attacks, complications) at 5 or 14 years, along with comparable quality of life outcomes for these two approaches.

Endoscopic balloon dilation (EPBD) compared to endoscopic sphincterotomy for extracting CBD stones has lower risk of bleeding and, if duration is >1 minute in one meta-analysis, is not associated with increased risk of pancreatitis. Optimal duration of dilation in a Chinese trial was 30 seconds (range 0 to 300 seconds) to minimize adverse effect without compromising successful stone extraction.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 25 RCTs found the two above procedures equally effective in stone removal at first attempt and there was no difference in overall stone clearance or pancreatitis when using a large (10 mm or greater) balloon. Rates of bleeding and cholecystitis were lower with EPBD. Authors of a meta-analysis of 18 studies with 2789 patients with large CBD stones concluded that stone removal rate was higher in the EPBD group vs endoscopic sphincterotomy (OR 2.68, 95 % CI 1.79 to 4.01 across all ERCP sessions) with fewer complications (OR 0.63, 95 % CI 0.47 to 0.85).
Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy combined with medical therapy can be considered in patients with radiolucent, solitary stones smaller than 2 cm, and a functional gallbladder.

Limited data based on five case-control studies showed that use of laparoscopic holmium laser lithotripsy was superior to laparoscopic bile duct exploration for treating complicated biliary calculus with respect to operative time, duration of hospitalization and rate of residual stone (OR 0.13).

In an RCT of 98 patients with cirrhosis and CBD stones undergoing endoscopic sphincterotomy, there were no differences in success rates between procedures followed by mechanical lithotripsy vs. large balloon dilation (93.8% and 98%, respectively) but more complications occurred in the lithotripsy group (16.3% vs 4.1%).

In a case series of 156 patients with difficult bile duct stones (i.e., one or more of: largest stone diameter ≥15 mm, failed prior stone clearance attempt, impacted, multiple, hepatic duct location, or located above a stricture), single peroral cholangioscopic-guided lithotripsy was successful in 80% (95% CI 73% to 86%). Serious adverse events occurred in 3 patients (1.9%, 95% CI 0.4% to 5.5%) including pancreatitis, perforation due to laser lithotripsy, and cholangitis (1 each) which resolved within 1 week.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 3 RCTs and 43 observational studies found no significant differences in successful clearance and adverse events rates between cholangioscopy-guided lithotripsy and conventional ERCP removal methods. Based on the observational studies, the successful endoscopic clearance rate was 88.3% (95% CI 86.9% to 90.7%), mean procedure time was 47.50±6 min per session, number of sessions to clear the bile duct was 1.5±0.18, and adverse event rate was 8.7% (95% CI 7% to 10.9%).

Transhepatic or transperitoneal cholecystostomy (or cholecystotomy) is a bile drainage procedure through catheter placement that is used in cases where cholecystectomy is deemed unsafe. In one case series of 13 patients with symptomatic cholelithiasis and multiple comorbidities who underwent cholecystostomy, radiology-operated cholecystoscopy with stone removal was successful in 11 patients. The mean duration between cholecystostomy and stone removal was 151 days and between stone removal and gallbladder catheter removal was 39 days.

Transcutaneous neuromodulation (TN) compared to sham-TN significantly reduced time to first flatulence (38.9 ± 4.0 vs. 24.9 ± 2.4 hour) and time to defecation (63.1 ± 4.5 vs. 42.5 ± 3.1 hour) in patients following cholecystectomy.

Although a low-fat diet is routinely recommended, high-quality evidence that it makes a difference is lacking. Two small physiologic studies suggest that meal composition has little effect on gall bladder function or stone formation.
Refer for surgical consultation any patient with symptoms related to the presence of gallstone disease.
Hospitalize patients with unremitting right upper quadrant pain and tenderness who are not able to tolerate oral fluids, and consider a cholecystectomy on the first available day.
Complications of gallstones include cholecystitis, pancreatitis, gallstone ileus, and cholangitis.

In an RCT of 232 patients in the Netherlands with severe gallstone pancreatitis without cholangitis, there was no difference in the primary endpoint of a composite of mortality or major complications between conservative treatment and urgent ERCP with sphincterotomy (44% vs 38%; RR 0.87, 95% CI 0.64-1.18).

Based on 5 RCTs with 644 patients with acute gallstone pancreatitis, there is no evidence that early routine ERCP significantly affects mortality or complications, although early ERCP should be considered in patients with co-existing cholangitis or biliary obstruction.

Caution should be exercised for patients with moderate to severe acute biliary pancreatitis due to the findings from a retrospective cohort study demonstrating higher mortality (15.6% vs. 0%) and morbidity (30.3% vs. 5.5%) for cholecystectomy within 48 hours vs. delayed cholecystectomy.

In a Korean study of 290 patients recovering from acute biliary pancreatitis, 19.3% developed recurrent pancreatobiliary complications (35 cases of acute pancreatitis, 11 of acute cholecystitis, and 10 of acute cholangitis). Risk of complications was higher among patients with smaller stones (5 mm or less) and when cholecystectomy was delayed more than 2 weeks compared with the early cholecystectomy group (45.5 vs 5.0%).

Gallstone ileus is a rare complication of cholelithiasis. Authors of a systematic review reported on 49 cases finding that the most common mechanism was a lost stone during cholecystectomy that eroded through the intestinal wall leading to bowel obstruction at a mean of 12.4 years from the initial surgery (range 10 days to 50 years).
Choledocholithiasis is the leading cause of cholangitis. Authors of a case series reported an incidence of approximately 5% in patients undergoing ERCP.

Cholangitis is clinically suspected by fever, right upper quadrant abdominal pain and jaundice (Charcot triad), although sensitivity is low as only 50% to 70% of patients develop all 3 symptoms; sepsis and mental status changes can occur and biliary dilation may be seen on imaging. Cholangitis is treated with early initiation of antibiotics (eg, amoxicillin/clavulanic acid or ceftriaxone with metronidazole) and biliary decompression.

Most patients with gallstones remain asymptomatic; patients develop symptoms at a rate of 1.5% to 2.0% per year and complications are rare (3%). In one cohort study, 12% of patients with untreated gallstones developed biliary colic over 10 years.

In an observational study from 9 family practices, 32 patients with asymptomatic gallstones were followed up for 5 years: 8 patients developed symptoms, 3 were lost to follow-up, and 7 died of other causes.

Acute cholecystitis develops in up to 10% of patients with symptomatic gallstones. In one study, only 35 of 69 patients (51%) with symptomatic gallstones randomized to observation eventually had surgery after a median of 5.6 years. In another study, 29.5% of the 217 patients randomized to observation underwent cholecystectomy by 2 years.

In one database study, 84 of 664 patients with symptomatic gallstones causing hospital admission were discharged without cholecystectomy and readmission occurred in 60.8% of them, with cholecystectomy eventually performed in 47.7%. Risk for future readmission was increased among those who had epigastric pain (hazard ratio [HR] 3.63, 95%CI 1.62-8.12), larger gallstones >10 mm (HR 4.11, 95% CI 1.18-14.3), and younger age (HR older age 0.97, 95% CI 0.95-0.998).
Gallstones appear to be a cofactor in the development of gallbladder cancer.

In one follow-up study of postoperative complications of cholecystectomy in 92 patients (median follow-up = 31.1 months), investigators found continued or new abdominal pain in 30.4%. Improvement occurred in abdominal bloating, dyspepsia, heartburn, fat intolerance, and nausea and vomiting, while no improvement was seen for diarrhea, constipation, or excessive flatus.

Similar symptom improvement is also seen after laparoscopic cholecystectomy. In one study with a median follow-up of 18 months, biliary pain was relieved in 99% of patients, with most showing improved nausea (98%), vomiting (96%), sour eructation (92%), belching (64%), flatulence (61%) and heartburn (59%). New symptoms included postprandial diarrhea (20%), heartburn (6%), belching (3.5%), sour eructation (1%) and vomiting (0.5%).
Postoperative infections occurred in 7.7% of Swedish patients following acute cholecystectomy; abscesses occurred in 2%.

CBD stones can recur even after cholecystectomy. In a Korean population study of 46,181 patients with CBD stones, first recurrence after endoscopic CBD removal was reported in 5228 (11.3%) patients; of 16,910 patients who also had gallstones, recurrence of CBD stones was 7.92% in the cholecystectomy group and 14.6% in the non-cholecystectomy group. Rates of second and third recurrence were high at 23.4 and 33.4%, respectively.

In one study, patients with preoperative symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS, indicated by the Manning criteria) showed less improvement in quality of life after laparoscopic cholecystectomy for gallstones than those without IBS.

Authors of two different meta-analyses found gallstones to be associated with significant risk of developing colonic adenoma (OR 2.26; 95% CI, 1.83-2.81) and rectal cancer (OR 1.33; 95% CI, 1.02-1.73).

In a network of case-control studies, a history of cholelithiasis vs. no such history was significantly associated with small intestinal (OR 3.96), prostate (OR 1.36), and kidney cancers (OR 1.57). There was also a higher risk of kidney cancer among Swedish patients with prior cholecystectomy (HR 1.17, 95% CI 1.12-1.22), especially if the cholecystectomy was performed before age 40 years (HR 1.55, 95% CI 1.39-1.72). Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 studies involving 80,403 individuals also found an association between cholelithiasis and an increased risk of prostate cancer (RR 1.35, 95%CI 1.17-1.56) based on moderate-quality evidence.

In a population-based study of ultrasound screening for gallstones in Copenhagen, of whom 6.8% had gallstones and 3.2% had cholecystectomy at baseline, there was a higher risk of pooled gastrointestinal cancers (11.2% vs 6.64%; hazard ratio [HR] 1.50; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.12-2.01) and right-side colon cancer (2.57% vs 0.96%; HR 2.04; 95% CI 1.10-3.78) among those with gallstone disease vs. those without at a median follow-up of 24.7 years. There was no increased risk for pancreatic, esophageal, gastric, pooled colorectal, left-side colon, sigmoid colon, or rectal cancers for those with gallstone disease.

In a Chinese database case-control study including 510,137 participants without cancer at baseline of whom 6% had symptomatic gallstone disease, during 10 years of follow-up, 17,598 developed GI cancer. Individuals with symptomatic GSD vs. those without GSD had adjusted hazard ratios of 1.13 (1.01-1.29) for colorectal, 2.01 (1.78-2.26) for liver, 3.70 (2.88-4.87) for gallbladder, 2.31 (1.78-3.07) for biliary tract, and 1.38 (1.18-1.74) for pancreatic cancer.

In a matched case-control study in Taiwan including 8265 adults, the incidence rate ratio (IRR) of subsequent pancreatic cancer at 6 or more months was higher in the cholelithiasis group (IRR 5.28) and higher for those in the no-intervention compared to the cholecystectomy group (IRR 3.21).
Asymptomatic stones are unlikely to cause difficulty (1%-2% develop symptoms each year).
Symptomatic stones can be managed with episodic pain medication, lithotripsy, medication, or surgery.

Laparoscopic and small-incision cholecystectomy are both appropriate after an episode of cholecystitis (within 72 hours is best), or for frequent symptoms or suspicious findings on ultrasound (calcified gallbladder).

In a study of 3254 pregnant women, 5.1% developed gallbladder sludge or stones by the second trimester, 7.9% by the third trimester, and 10.2% by 4 weeks to 6 weeks postpartum. Regression of sludge was common.
Cholecystectomy was performed on 0.8% within the first year postpartum.
There are no prospective trials comparing early cholecystectomy with medical management in pregnant women.
Surgery is generally reserved for pregnant women with recurrent or unrelenting biliary pain refractory to medical management or with complications related to gallstones.

Among pregnant women undergoing ERCP, authors of a meta-analysis of 27 studies with 1307 patients found a pooled event rate for overall adverse outcomes of 15.9% (95% CI 13.2% to 19.1%) with no differences in event rate for procedures done with or without radiation. The pooled event rate for fetal adverse outcomes was 5.4% (95% CI 3.5% to 8.3%) and for maternal pregnancy-related adverse events was 6.1% (95% CI 4% to 9.3%).

Gallstones are uncommon in children; stones are more likely to be pigment stones. In a case series of 404 patients at a single institution from 2005 to 2008, obesity and Hispanic ethnicity were independent risk factors for nonhemolytic gallstone disease.

Obesity (vs. normal or underweight) was found to be a significant risk factor for gallstones in a large population-based study of children with adjusted odds ratios of gallstones for overweight, moderate obesity, and extreme obesity in boys of 1.46 (0.94%-2.27%), 1.83 (1.17%-2.85%), and 3.10 (1.99%-4.83%) and in girls 2.73 (2.18%-3.42%), 5.75 (4.62%-7.17%), and 7.71 (6.13%-9.71%), respectively.

Laparoscopic cholecystectomy can be used safely and effectively in children with biliary colic. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 114 studies including 76,524 children (average age 12 years) who underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy for cholelithiasis (68.4% in 66 studies) or cholecystitis (59.2% in 53 studies) found an overall postoperative complication rate of 3.4%. Major complications were uncommon and included bile duct injury (0.4%) and intra- or post-operative bleeding (0.9%). The conversion rate to open procedure was 2%.

Authors of a systematic review of 24 papers with 2783 children following laparoscopic cholecystectomy found reported complications occurred in 3.3% and included wound issues (n = 24), perforation (n = 14), bleeds (n = 13), biliary tree complications (n = 9), and sickle cell crisis (n = 8). Seventeen patients (18.3%) required re-intervention; 15 surgical and two endoscopic.

In a cohort study of children undergoing cholecstectomy for uncomplicated cholelithiasis, surgical site infections were less common in those receiving antibiotic prophylaxis (largely cefazolin), 0.9% vs 3.7% (aOR 0.28, 95% CI 0.11-0.70).
